body.heading: Lighter than air, literally
paragraphs: A hot-air balloon floats for the same reason a beach ball pops up underwater: it is lighter than what it displaces. The balloon's envelope holds a huge volume of air, and a propane burner heats that air so it expands — some escapes through the open bottom, leaving fewer, lighter molecules inside.

Hot air is less dense than the cool air outside, so the total weight of balloon, basket and passengers becomes less than the weight of the outside air they displace. Buoyancy — the upward push of the surrounding air — wins, and the balloon rises.

body.heading: Up, down, and nothing else
paragraphs: The pilot controls only height directly: fire the burner to climb, or let the air cool — or open a vent at the top to spill hot air — to descend. There is no engine pushing the balloon forward and no rudder to steer with.

Steering means choosing an altitude where the wind blows the way you want to go. Winds at different heights often differ in direction, so a skilled pilot climbs and sinks through layers of air like a sailor choosing currents.

body.heading: A gentle giant
paragraphs: The scale is grand: a typical sport balloon's envelope holds around 77,000 cubic feet — about 2,200 cubic metres — of air, enough to fill a small house, and the whole aircraft may lift half a tonne. All that lift comes from air warmed by only a few tens of degrees.

Flights favour dawn and dusk, when surface winds are calmest and the air is stable. The balloon travels exactly at wind speed, so passengers feel no breeze at all — the stillness is one of the strangest parts of the ride.

description: Heat the air inside a balloon and it expands and lightens until the whole craft weighs less than the air it displaces.
